name: stairs rise 3 w2 reverse cut through a north-facing grass cliff, seen from above descending away from the viewer from the terrace lip
label: relief-cuts-rev/grass-steps/stairs-h3-w2

refSet.reason: 칩셋 relief-cuts-rev 의 화풍 기준 묶음이 없다

surfaces.part: stair treads (repeating steps, each about 5 rows: light nosing row, 2-3 rows of grey tread, 1 dark edge row)
brown earth cliff walls at left and right edges

answer.evidence: The column scan at x=8, 16 and 23 shows the same 5-row cycle all the way down: a light row (L 197-223), grey tread rows (L 118-145), then a 1-row dark line (L 52-63). The stairs descend away from the viewer, so only the treads are seen from above. The dark rows are 1-row edge lines, not vertical risers, so there is no front face of 3 or more rows. The brown strips at the left and right edges are narrow cliff sides, not a receding isometric side face. The whole 32-row silhouette is a flat top-down staircase, not a standing volume.

styleAnswer.evidence: Each step has a bright lip highlight, a light tread, a mid tone and a darker riser shadow, about 5 lightness steps, close to the paving reference. The measured facts support this: 9 visible tones per tile against 3 for grass and 7 for paving, and 0% near-flat coverage. Only 29% of dark edge pixels are neutral, and the brown-tinted side edges beside the steps read as material-tone outlines, not a uniform black sticker line. The weak point is texture. The step faces lean on clean banded gradients with little stone grain compared with the cobbled paving reference, so I rate texture 'some', not 'rich'. The piece still holds up next to the references on tone count, edge treatment and absence of flat fills.

surfaces.part: stair treads (repeating 5-row steps, light nosing row then grey tread rows)
dark 1-row gap/shadow line under each step

answer.evidence: The column scans show the same 5-row cycle all the way down: a light row (L about 197-223), 1-3 mid-grey rows (L 118-145), then a 1-row dark line (L about 52). This reads as a descending flight seen from above, with each step a light edge, a grey tread and a dark shadow or gap. The dark line is only 1 row, and the risers face away from the viewer, so there is no vertical front face of 3 or more rows. The 32-row full-width silhouette fills the tile like a flat top-down slab, with no side face and no standing volume. The 32-row figure is the whole tile, not a single surface, and no one tread is a separate main top. The brown strips at the edges are the cliff and earth, not a front face.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a small stair strip of light grey treads with brown side rails, sitting on an empty dark slate backdrop. The measured facts look fine: 9 visible tones per tile against 7 for paving and 3 for grass, 0% near-flat coverage, and only 29% neutral dark edge pixels, so the outline leans tinted. By eye the picture is weaker than the numbers. Each tread is a smooth bar with a light top edge, a mid face and a dark underline, roughly 4 value steps. It has none of the per-stone shading, speckle or grain that the cobble paving carries, and none of the grass tufts or clumps. The stair reads as a clean, flat, sticker-like object rather than a ground patch cut into a grass cliff. The grass cliff and terrace are not drawn, so the 4x3 ground patch is not delivered. A careful artist would not accept it next to the references without it looking flatter and thinner.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate has 9 visible tones per tile, against 3 for the grass reference and 7 for the paving reference. Near-flat coverage is 0%, the same as both references. Only 29% of its dark edge pixels are neutral, so the dark brown side walls and dark grey step edges mostly lean toward the material. The outline is therefore not a black sticker line, though the grey edges are partly neutral, which is why I call it mixed.
